title: Parallel Compilation
concept: Parallel compilation uses all CPU cores to compile independent modules simultaneously — turning an 8-core machine into an 8x faster build.
why: Modern CPUs have many cores but compilers default to one. Parallel compilation distributes work across all cores, dramatically reducing build times.
theory:
## Multi-Core Builds

```sh
# Default: use all available cores
xiom build

# Explicit: use 4 parallel jobs
xiom build --parallel 4

# Single-threaded: useful for debugging
xiom build --parallel 1
```

### How It Works

```
Sequential build (8 modules):
[A] → [B] → [C] → [D] → [E] → [F] → [G] → [H]
Total: sum of all compile times

Parallel build (8 modules, 4 cores):
Core 1: [A] → [E]
Core 2: [B] → [F]
Core 3: [C] → [G]
Core 4: [D] → [H]
Total: time of longest core
```

### Scheduling

The compiler uses the dependency graph to schedule work:

1. **Root modules first**: modules with no dependencies
2. **Fan-out**: as dependencies complete, dependents are queued
3. **Work stealing**: idle cores grab work from busy cores' queues
4. **Link last**: linking is single-threaded (the bottleneck)

### Parallelism Limits

Not everything is parallelizable:

| Phase | Parallel? | Notes |
|-------|-----------|-------|
| Parsing | Yes | Different files are independent |
| Type checking | Partial | Module-local checking is parallel, cross-module is not |
| Code generation | Yes | Each function is independent |
| Optimization | Yes | Per-function optimization is parallel |
| Linking | No | Single-threaded (use LLD or mold for speed) |

### Measuring Speedup

```sh
xiom build --time --parallel 1   # Baseline
xiom build --time --parallel 8   # Parallel
# Compare the output times
```

### Recommended Settings

```toml
# xiom.toml
[build]
parallel = 0  # 0 = auto-detect CPU cores
```

Rule of thumb: `parallel = CPU_CORES` for fastest builds. `parallel = CPU_CORES - 1` if you want to keep one core free.
syntax_ref:
xiom build --parallel 8     # Use 8 cores
xiom build --parallel 1     # Single-threaded
# xiom.toml:
[build]
parallel = 0               # Auto-detect
tips: Default auto-detection (parallel=0) is usually optimal — the compiler knows your hardware
Linking is the bottleneck — use mold (Linux) or lld (macOS/Windows) for faster linking
Structure code into many SMALL modules — more parallelism opportunities
Don't set parallel > CPU cores — context switching overhead erases gains
common_mistakes: Setting parallel to 16 on a 4-core machine — hyperthreading doesn't double compile throughput
Forgetting that linking is single-threaded — a huge binary with many modules spends most time linking
Not measuring actual speedup — more parallelism doesn't always mean faster builds
